title: Surfside Commerce Cost Pathways - Redwood Intake
summary: Initial cost/unit economics discovery for a commerce personalization inference workflow. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment tradeoffs, per-token pricing, batching/caching levers, peak-hour provisioning for flash sales, and security/PCI constraints. Agreed next steps: share a tailored unit-econ spreadsheet, security pack, and schedule a Dedicated capacity pricing run and small-scale benchmark during a simulated flash sale window.
topics: Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private for predictable peak
security: PCI scope and BYOK/KMS options
pilot/benchmark plan for flash sale scenario
next_steps: Redwood to send tailored unit-econ spreadsheet and model-cost scenarios
Send SOC2 + security pack and brief PCI notes
Schedule dedicated capacity pricing call with finance (week of 5/11)
Set up 2-hour benchmark window during off-hours to simulate flash sale (customer to confirm date)

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-03
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Priya Narang (Redwood SE), Sam Wu (notes), Daniel Park (CTO - Surfside), Meera Singh (ML Eng Lead), Omar Reyes (Infra), Lena Ortiz (Product)

[00:00:03] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, appreciate it. quick one, i'm alex, i'm on the account team. priya is our SE, she'll run through the cost levers and we'll do a few live examples.
[00:00:12] Daniel: yep thanks alex. short background — we run personalization and dynamic creative for our checkout flow. big spikes around flash sales, black friday-ish peaks, and we need to understand per-request cost if we push more personalized prompts to the model.
[00:00:25] Priya: great, that helps. first question for you, daniel: what does a typical request look like? is it a short prompt (single-line), or are you doing multi-turn session state for each user?
[00:00:34] Meera: it's a mix. 60% are single-shot re-rank and product suggestion prompts ~150 tokens input, 200 tokens output. 40% are session-backed personalization with a 2-3 turn history; average seq len for those is 600 tokens.
[00:00:47] Alex: perfect — that already tells us batching and prefix caching will change the math a lot. for single-shot calls you can often benefit from batching at the inference edge, for session-backed you want KV cache and pinned sessions in Dedicated to save tokens.
[00:00:59] Omar: can you explain the pinned sessions bit? we assume stateful sessions mean more memory and cost?
[00:01:06] Priya: sure. pinned sessions mean we keep the KV cache warm on the same pod/gpu so that each continued turn avoids re-encoding full history. that reduces per-request compute. on hosted we can do warm caching but eviction is more likely during spikes; on Dedicated you can reserve capacity so KV stays resident.
[00:01:22] [00:01:22] Alex: quick interjection — for budgeting, we usually show cost-per-1M tokens and then adjust by effective tokens after cache hits and batching.
[00:01:30] Lena: what are the typical numbers? like what would 1M tokens cost on hosted vs dedicated?
[00:01:36] Priya: i'll give you ranges — ballpark only: hosted API per-token price depends on model family. for a mid-size open model it's typically $X to $Y per 1M input+output tokens on the hosted tier — to avoid quoting exact public competitor numbers here, i'll say "hosted: higher unit price but zero infra ops". Dedicated is lower per-token compute because customers commit reserved capacity, so effective per-1M can be 25-40% lower depending on utilization and model quantization. private/on-prem has lowest incremental compute cost but highest fixed platform/license and ops overhead.
[00:02:09] Daniel: 25-40% is big. how does batching change that? we expect a lot of small requests, especially in checkout, which hurts latency.
[00:02:17] Priya: batching improves GPU utilization. if you can batch small single-shot calls (like re-rank calls) you can reduce per-token cost by 20-60% depending on request size and batch window. but batching adds latency overhead — our runtime supports dynamic batching with a target latency SLO: you can set a max wait time of, say, 10ms or 50ms; shorter wait = less batching = higher cost.
[00:02:38] Omar: our SLO for checkout personalization is 120ms p95 end-to-end. can batching fit?
[00:02:43] Priya: network + pre/post-process + model = you have maybe 40-60ms budget for model. with 50ms batch window we can still often meet 120ms p95 for small models, but for large context lengths and larger models you may need Dedicated with local networking and fewer hops.
[00:02:57] Alex: and that maps to a cost trade — you accept a slightly higher infrastructure commit (Dedicated) to maintain low latency and lower per-token price at scale.
[00:03:05] [00:03:05] Meera: what about KV caching numbers? for our session flows we see repeated user context elements — how aggressive should we be with caching?
[00:03:12] Priya: if you can cache prefixes and reuse them 3-5x per session, effective tokens dropped a lot. example: an incoming session has 600 tokens; with prefix caching of 300 tokens used across turns, you only pay compute for delta tokens most of the time. in practice you measure cache hit rate; we commonly see 40-60% reduction on session-heavy workloads.
[00:03:31] Daniel: ok that helps. what about model size and quantization? can we run a quantized variant and still keep quality?
[00:03:37] Priya: yes — Redwood Optimize will recommend quantized variants per workload. at inference we support 8-bit and mixed quantization; quality regression is model/workload dependent. we run eval suites to measure BLEU/nlg metrics and custom prompt checks. typical trade: 8-bit gives 1.6–2x speed and lower cost, often with small quality hit; we flag regressions if evals dip under your acceptance threshold.
[00:03:57] Alex: random note — if you need guaranteed quality we recommend canary on live traffic + fallback to higher-fidelity model if metrics degrade.
[00:04:05] Lena: about private/on-prem — our payments team is sensitive because of PCI implications. does Redwood have a path to keep inference outside scope?
[00:04:12] Alex: short answer: yes. Dedicated with VPC/private peering + BYOK can keep tokens/data from touching Redwood's multitenant control plane. for full PCI scope removal you might need on-prem or a customer-managed environment; we'll share our PCI guidance doc.
[00:04:25] Meera: do you support HSM/KMS for keys?
[00:04:29] Priya: yes — KMS integrations and BYOK for Dedicated and Private. audit logs are available and we can configure retention windows. we'll send the SOC2 packet and a PCI note as requested.
[00:04:39] [00:04:39] Daniel: switching back to cost examples — could we walk through a sample math for 10k RPS baseline vs a flash-sale 100k RPS for 10 minutes? that's the wildcard for us.
[00:04:48] Priya: sure — i'll do simplified math. baseline 10k RPS with 70% single-shot (200 tokens total) and 30% session (average 600 tokens): effective tokens per second — you do the math — but the key is: at baseline a hosted solution with batching yields moderate unit costs; for the 100k spike, hosted will either autoscale (higher bill) or request fallback to smaller models. Dedicated lets you provision burst capacity and reserve capacity for predictable peaks with lower incremental cost.
[00:05:15] Alex: to make it concrete, we'll show this in the unit-econ spreadsheet: run three scenarios — hosted with autoscale, hosted with fallback policy, and dedicated with reserved burst pools — and compare per-hour bill and effective cost per 1k active users.
[00:05:29] Omar: curious: how does Redwood handle automatic fallback during capacity congestion? we want a graceful degradation strategy.
[00:05:35] Priya: smart routing — you can set policies to fall back to a smaller architecture (quantized or smaller model), or route to a lower-cost region. Redwood console lets you define route policies and automatic fallback thresholds. we also support weighted rollouts so you can reduce model size on a percentage of traffic and monitor quality before full switch.
[00:05:50] Meera: hmm, quality cliffs worry me — we've had bad re-rank regressions before. what's the observability?
[00:05:55] Priya: console provides token-level latency, per-route quality signals (custom evals), and prompt-level logs (redacted) so you can detect regressions. alerts can be tied to prompt-set metrics.
[00:06:06] [00:06:06] Daniel: okay, last major area — pricing transparency. we need line-item clarity: base model compute, memory footprint, dedicated seat/commit fees, storage, and networking.
[00:06:15] Alex: totally. we usually produce a pricing sheet that breaks out: model compute per-1M tokens (hosted rate), Dedicated reservation monthly fee + effective per-token charge, storage for KV cache if large, and egress/network where applicable. we'll show an example with your numbers.
[00:06:28] Lena: who signs off on dedicated pricing? finance or an account exec?
[00:06:32] Alex: dedicated pricing for reserved capacity usually goes through our sales + finance team; commitments change the per-token numbers. we'll loop in finance on the next call.
[00:06:40] Omar: a practical question — for the flash-sale 100k spike, how quickly can you spin up burst GPUs?
[00:06:46] Priya: hosted autoscale can respond within minutes but it's not instant — cold start and image pull adds time. Dedicated with pre-warmed burst pools is the only way to guarantee sub-minute response for big spikes. you can keep a small burst pool in standby to cover the first minutes.
[00:06:58] [00:06:58] Meera: do you have examples of customers who've used that pattern?
[00:07:02] Alex: yes — a retail customer used dedicated reserved pools and a 10% standby burst to handle promotional spikes; they reduced overprovisioning by 60% versus always-on capacity.
[00:07:10] Daniel: okay good. i also want to capture potential objections from our procurement team — length of commitment and exit terms.
[00:07:16] Alex: common ask. we offer flexible commit terms — monthly or annual — with sliding discounts. exit terms are negotiated; we'll include standard language in the pricing packet we send.
[00:07:24] [00:07:24] Lena: a small thing — can we get a rough TCO showing host vs dedicated vs private for a 12-month horizon with your suggested utilization numbers?
[00:07:31] Priya: yes, that's exactly what we'll deliver in the unit-econ spreadsheet. we'll model utilization at 40%, 70%, and 90% for dedicated to show sensitivity.
[00:07:39] Omar: network egress — are there surprises there? like inter-region costs.
[00:07:43] Priya: avoid cross-region inference where possible. we'll call out egress and peering costs; dedicated VPC peering reduces surprise egress but there are provider charges at the cloud level.
[00:07:53] [00:07:53] Meera: for the benchmark, what data do you need from us?
[00:07:56] Priya: sample prompts, sequence length distributions, RPS curves (baseline and spike), and any eval prompts for quality thresholds. you already gave the sequence numbers; if you can share a few anonymized sample prompts and RPS curve we'll set up a small synthetic load test.
[00:08:10] Daniel: sounds good. we'll redact PII, but that should be fine.
[00:08:13] Alex: great. last minute notes — we'll include a section where we show how batching window affects latency and cost with a small chart (example values), and another section that calculates effective tokens after cache hits.
[00:08:24] [00:08:24] Meera: one process question — if we opt for Dedicated, who operates day-to-day: your infra team or ours?
[00:08:29] Alex: Redwood operates the runtime; you get a private control plane for Dedicated (and optional private deployments for full control). day-to-day ops can be co-managed. security-sensitive customers sometimes run on-prem for full separation.
[00:08:41] Omar: do you publish latency SLOs for hosted?
[00:08:44] Priya: hosted has published targets in our docs, but enterprise SLA is part of Dedicated contracts. we'll point you to the SLO docs.
[00:08:53] [00:08:53] Daniel: ok i'm satisfied with the overview. final ask — can you send a simple one-page 'decision rubric' that maps our requirements to the recommended deployment (hosted vs dedicated vs private)?
[00:09:01] Alex: yes, we'll include that in the follow-up packet.
[00:09:05] Priya: and to reiterate the benchmark plan: we'll propose a 2-hour synthetic flash-sale window test, execute in a non-prod environment, and collect latency and cost metrics.
[00:09:13] Meera: that will be useful.
[00:09:16] [00:09:16] (small side chatter and time checks)
[00:09:22] Alex: ok wrapping up — quick recap of action items and owners (i'll read them out). alex — send unit-econ sheet, priya — set up benchmark plan, meera — provide sample prompts and RPS curve, daniel — confirm test date, sam — attach SOC2 / security summary in the notes.
[00:09:38] Daniel: thanks everyone. good discussion.
[00:09:41] Alex: thanks all, we'll follow up by eod tuesday with the packet.

Notes and artifacts referenced:
- "unit-econ-template.xlsx" (Alex to send)
- "redwood-security-packet.pdf" (Sam to attach)
- Bench plan doc link (Priya to create)

End of transcript.
